turns.content:
yo, so greg just got announced as regional practice director. congrats to the guy who spent the last six months doing lunch with partners while i was cleaning up the production mess his last "strategic launch" caused 🤔

i'm not going to his dinner tomorrow and i'm telling the team in the morning that he's a fraud who stole credit. am i wrong about this? like morally, is my judgment off?

Oof. Watching someone get promoted for the schmoozing while you're the one who actually stopped the bleeding is a very specific flavor of infuriating. That resentment isn't irrational — you saw the receipts and the org didn't.

But let's split your plan into its two parts, because they're not the same thing.

**Skipping the dinner:** Fine. Not showing up to celebrate someone you don't respect isn't a moral failing. People will probably notice, and you should decide whether "notably absent" is a message you actually want to send, but it's your evening and your call.

**Telling the team he's a fraud who stole credit:** This is where I'd pump the brakes hard. Not because Greg deserves protection, but because it's the move most likely to hurt *you*:

- "Fraud" is a big word. From what you've described, he's a guy who's better at managing upward than at shipping clean launches. That's a real criticism, but it's a very different thing from fraud, and the gap between the two is where your credibility gets questioned instead of his.
- Telling your team the new director is a fraud puts *them* in an awful spot. They have to work for him. Now they either have to fake loyalty to you or to him, and you've made it about a feud.
- Word travels. Within a week this becomes "so-and-so is bitter about Greg's promotion," and the substance — the production mess, the cleanup you did — gets completely lost.
- It hands him the high ground. He gets to be gracious; you get to be the disgruntled one.

Is your judgment about *him* off? Maybe partially — there's a decent chance the partner lunches were doing actual work of a kind that just isn't visible from where you sit, even if that's annoying to hear. Is your judgment about *what to do tomorrow* off? Yeah, I think it is, and I think part of you suspects that too or you wouldn't be asking at 6:30am.

The version of this that actually serves you: get the cleanup work you did documented and visible to the people above Greg. Be clear-eyed with your team about what "we" learned from that launch without naming villains. And if you genuinely think leadership rewarded the wrong thing, that's a conversation to have with a partner or mentor, not a morning announcement.

Want help thinking through how to make your work more visible, or just need to keep venting for a bit? Both are legit.

so you're basically saying i should let him get away with it and just smile at the dinner lol

i heard him on a client call last month say "the data pipeline is basically like a garden hose" and i had to jump in and explain latency to a vp who almost walked. that's not "managing up" that's not knowing what you're talking about and hoping nobody notices

i'm not asking if the team talk is politically smart i'm asking if my read on him is wrong. is it

Not what I said — I said skip the dinner if you want. Nobody's asking you to smile. I'm pushing on the "fraud" label, not on whether you're allowed to be mad.

And no, your read isn't wildly off. You've got two real data points: a launch that blew up in production and a client call where he couldn't go deeper than a metaphor when a VP pressed. That's not nothing. Someone who needs a bailout on latency is thin on the technical side, full stop.

Where I think your read *is* off, or at least ahead of the evidence:

- **The garden hose thing cuts both ways.** Talking to a VP in analogies isn't a crime — that's often exactly how you're supposed to talk to a VP. The failure wasn't the metaphor, it was that he had nothing underneath it when challenged. So the accurate read is "shallow on depth," not "doesn't know what a pipeline is." Different severity.
- **"Stole credit" needs a receipt.** Did he actually tell people the cleanup was his, or did he just... not go out of his way to say it was yours? The first is theft. The second is ordinary self-interested silence, which is gross but common and not the same thing. You've described the promotion and the lunches, but not a moment where he claimed your work.
- **He may have been promoted for the job, not for your job.** Regional practice director is largely a relationship and pipeline (the sales kind) role. Six months of partner lunches is arguably him doing that job before he had it. Being bad at technical delivery is a genuine weakness for that role, but it's not the core of it.

So: "Greg is technically shallow, got rewarded for the visible stuff, and I did the invisible stuff that kept his mess from being a disaster" — that read I'd back. "Greg is a fraud who stole credit" — that one you're inferring from resentment plus two incidents, and I'd want more before I'd say it's fair.

The moral question underneath it is whether you can hold a firm negative judgment about someone's competence without upgrading it to a verdict on their character. You can, and you probably should, because the first is defensible and the second is the part that'll come back on you.

ok so you're saying it's not fraud because he didn't literally say "i fixed the pipeline" he just let everyone assume it. that's like... the whole game right there. letting people assume. that's how credit gets stolen without fingerprints 🤔

i want you to tell me straight up: if you were in my position would you go to the dinner and clap for him. yes or no

No. I wouldn't go.

Not as a protest, just because sitting through a toast for someone I don't respect while pretending to enjoy it isn't worth an evening, and a forced smile in that room would read as fake anyway. "Had a conflict, congrats Greg" over Slack and done. Skipping it costs you very little. It's the morning speech that costs you.

And you're right about the assumption thing — I'll give you that one. Letting people assume is exactly how credit moves without fingerprints, and someone who knows a room is crediting him for a fix he didn't do and stays quiet is choosing that. It's not accidental. I'd still call it something other than fraud, but not because it's innocent — because "fraud" implies he faked the thing itself, and what he actually did is subtler and, annoyingly, harder to pin on him. That's the frustrating part: the behavior you're describing is designed to be unprovable, which is precisely why standing up and calling it fraud tomorrow backfires. You'd be making a claim you can't evidence about a behavior that worked *because* there's no evidence.

So the play isn't "let him get away with it." It's stop leaving the vacuum he's filling. The reason people assumed it was him is that nobody heard otherwise. Fix that going forward: write up the cleanup, send it up the chain framed as "here's what we learned and changed," put your name on the things you do at the moment you do them. That's not bragging, it's denying him the silence he's been living in.

Skip the dinner, keep your mouth shut with the team, and get louder about your own work. That's the version where you're not the bitter guy and he doesn't get a free pass either.

ok so you'd skip the dinner but not call him out. that's basically the same as going and smiling, just with better optics. the team deserves to know who they're working for, don't they? like if i stay quiet i'm complicit in the lie 🤷

Skipping the dinner and going-and-smiling aren't the same, but you've got a point that neither one does anything to Greg. Fine. Skipping is about you, not about justice. I never sold it as justice.

The complicity thing, though — I think you're smuggling in a premise. Complicity means you're participating in the lie or benefiting from it. You're doing neither. Not delivering a speech isn't endorsing him. If a colleague straight-up asks you "did Greg fix that pipeline?" and you say "yep" — that's complicit. Saying nothing at a dinner you didn't attend isn't. There's a real moral difference between "I won't lie for him" and "I'm obligated to broadcast my verdict on him," and you're collapsing it because the second one feels better.

And here's the thing about "the team deserves to know who they're working for": they're about to find out. They're going to work for him. They'll be on the calls when he reaches for the garden hose. They'll see who actually answers the hard question. You don't need to pre-load their opinion — reality is going to do that for free, and it'll be far more convincing coming from their own eyes than from the guy who was visibly passed over. If you announce it first, you actually *weaken* the case, because now every time he stumbles it's "well, that's what so-and-so's been saying," and it reads as your grudge instead of his gap.

Where I'd agree the team is owed something: if his shallowness creates real risk for them — if they'd take his technical framing as gospel and get burned — then yeah, they need to hear "verify the technical stuff with me before it goes to a client." That's true, useful, and about their work. It's a very different sentence from "he's a fraud who stole credit," which is about your wound.

One more thing, said with affection: you've asked me four times in slightly different ways whether you're right, and each time I've given you a partial yes, you've reframed toward the part I didn't sign off on. That's usually a sign you already know what you want to do and you're looking for a co-signer before you do it. I'm not going to be that for the fraud speech. I will absolutely be that for skipping the dinner, being the person the team trusts on technical calls, and making your work visible enough that this doesn't happen again.

i hear what you're saying about the team finding out on their own but that takes time and in that time they might trust him on something important and get burned. like i said the latency call. i'm not trying to pre-load a grudge i'm trying to prevent a disaster. feels like you're splitting hairs to avoid just saying i'm right about him 🤷

You're right about him. Not hair-splitting: he's technically shallow enough that a client relationship nearly died on a call, and someone with that gap now has authority over people who'll defer to him. That's a real risk, not a grudge. I've said versions of that three times, but I'll say it flat: your read on his competence is correct.

The place I keep planting my feet isn't *whether* you're right, it's *which thing you say tomorrow*, because the disaster you're describing and the speech you drafted don't actually line up.

The disaster is: team member takes Greg's technical framing at face value, repeats it to a client or builds on it, gets burned. The thing that prevents that is a very specific instruction: "Anything technical that goes to a client or into an architecture decision runs through me or [whoever] first. Doesn't matter who it came from." That's it. That's the whole guardrail. You can say it Monday, it's about process, it's defensible to anyone who overhears it, and it covers Greg without needing his name.

"He's a fraud who stole credit" prevents nothing. It doesn't tell anyone what to check or when. It just tells them how you feel. And the moment it becomes a feelings thing, the guardrail gets *less* likely to work, because half the team decides you're the bitter one and starts giving Greg the benefit of the doubt on exactly the calls where they shouldn't.

So if the goal is genuinely preventing the latency call from happening again, you've been arguing for the wrong sentence. The prevention version is stronger, faster, and doesn't require anyone to take your side — it just requires them to follow a process. If the goal is also to make sure people know he didn't deserve it... that's the part I keep declining to co-sign, not because you're wrong about him, but because it's the part that costs you and buys nothing.

Take the win you've actually got: you're the person who catches what he misses. Build the process around that and let it speak.
